plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and fatty liver: what MASLD and MASH are, how excess weight and insulin resistance are linked to liver fat, what the randomized SYNERGY-NASH Phase 2 trial found on liver biopsy, what the SURPASS-3 MRI substudy found about liver fat in type 2 diabetes, and why fatty liver isn't an approved use for tirzepatide
plan.angle: Keep the brief as written, with these changes. 1) Opening sentence 1: 'If you've been told you have a fatty liver and you're wondering whether tirzepatide helps: in one randomized Phase 2 trial in adults with MASH and moderate or advanced liver scarring, more people on tirzepatide than on placebo had their MASH resolve on a liver biopsy after fifty-two weeks. It isn't an approved use, so it's one to talk through with your doctor.' 2) Primary result: 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% on the lowest, middle and highest tirzepatide doses tested. Say no mg values on screen or in narration. The per-arm n comes from the NEJM paper. Fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of MASH was a secondary outcome: 30% vs 55%, 51% and 51%. Never describe MASH resolution as 'inflammation went away'. 3) SURPASS-3 MRI: present it as a separate substudy in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor. It measured liver fat content by MRI over 52 weeks, comparing the two higher tirzepatide arms pooled vs insulin degludec. Use the absolute percentage-point change exactly as the PubMed abstract gives it, and don't present it as resolution or fibrosis data. 4) Approval chapter: quote Section 1 of the live Mounjaro PI (including the major adverse cardiovascular events indication if it appears on the live label) and of the live Zepbound PI (including obstructive sleep apnea). Read the revised dates on DailyMed. Credit FDA in one neutral line: semaglutide (Wegovy) is approved in the US for adults with noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. No comparison, no ranking, no switching. 5) Keep all safety lines, the 'recommended, not proven on tirzepatide' framing for lifestyle habits, and the hepatologist question list. Thumbnail 'LIVER FAT?' with one calm, fully drawn, labelled character, no organ imagery and no body-shaming. Verified sources so far: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38856224/.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and Fatty Liver: Does It Help?
plan.why: Fills today's dropped long-video slot with a topic the channel hasn't covered. It rests on settled randomized evidence (NEJM SYNERGY-NASH, SURPASS-3 MRI) plus label Section 1, so it can pass the fact-check first time, and drug-name searches ('Mounjaro fatty liver') keep bringing in viewers over time. | fact-check: The topic is sound, fits the channel and has strong evidence behind it. I checked these points: (1) SYNERGY-NASH (Loomba et al., NEJM 2024; PubMed 38856224, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38856224/) was a Phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding trial. It enrolled 190 adults with biopsy-confirmed noncirrhotic MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, treated for 52 weeks. MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis was 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% across the three tirzepatide arms. Improvement of at least one fibrosis stage without worsening of MASH was a secondary endpoint: 30% vs 55%, 51% and 51%. (2) Tirzepatide still has no US approval for MASLD or MASH. Its approved uses are type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro, which also has a 2026 approval to lower major cardiovascular event risk in type 2 diabetes), chronic weight management (Zepbound) and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity (Zepbound). (3) FDA approved semaglutide (Wegovy) in August 2025 for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis (F2–F3). Fixes needed: (a) The sample opening says 'liver inflammation resolve'. That is inaccurate: MASH resolution on biopsy is a composite histology endpoint, not just inflammation. (b) The angle asks for per-arm results but also bans dose numbers. Keep the ban and describe the arms without milligrams. (c) In SURPASS-3 MRI (Gastaldelli et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2022), the primary liver-fat comparison pooled two tirzepatide arms against insulin degludec. Say so, and report the result as a change in liver fat content measured by MRI-PDFF, not 'fatty liver resolved'. Confirm the exact figures on PubMed before scripting. (d) The FDA line for Wegovy must keep 'noncirrhotic' and 'moderate to advanced fibrosis' and say it is used alongside diet and exercise, as FDA prints it. (e) The SURPASS-CVOT approval may be missing from older label text. Quote Section 1 from the live Mounjaro PI and the live Zepbound PI on DailyMed and use their actual revised dates. Everything else in the angle (no 'reverses' or 'cures', guideline habits marked 'recommended', a clinician line, the pancreatitis emergency wording, the low-blood-sugar caveat) is correct; keep it. I found no misinformation or strike risk once these fixes are in.

package.description:
Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area, your abdomen, that will not go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your abdomen to your back. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Fatty liver, MASLD and MASH are not an approved use for tirzepatide.

Quick answer: In SYNERGY-NASH, a Phase 2 trial in 190 adults with MASH and stage 2–3 scarring, MASH resolved without scarring getting worse at 52 weeks in 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% on the lowest, middle and highest tirzepatide doses tested. As a secondary outcome, scarring improved by at least one stage without MASH getting worse in 30% vs 55%, 51% and 51%. In an open-label SURPASS-3 MRI substudy in type 2 diabetes, liver fat fell more on tirzepatide than on insulin degludec. MRI measures fat, not MASH or scarring.

Sources:
1. Loomba R et al. NEJM 2024: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38856224/
2. Gastaldelli A et al. 2022: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35468325/
3. Zepbound label, rev 8/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html#pi

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
package.pinned_comment: The result we flagged as the surprise: in SYNERGY-NASH (adults with MASH and stage 2–3 scarring, 52 weeks), as a secondary outcome, scarring improved by at least one stage without MASH getting worse in 30% on placebo vs 55%, 51% and 51% on the lowest, middle and highest tirzepatide doses tested. Unlike MASH resolution, it didn't climb with dose. It's one Phase 2 trial: a signal to test, not a final answer. If you take tirzepatide, stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area, your abdomen, that will not go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your abdomen to your back. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Fatty liver isn't an approved use for tirzepatide. Save this for your next appointment. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and Fatty Liver: Does It Help?
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario + stakes: sentence 1 echoes the searched question (fatty liver + tirzepatide), the biopsy answer (MASH resolved without scarring getting worse) lands by about 15 s, the headline numbers (10% vs 44/56/62%) land at about 21–30 s, and one open loop (the result that did not climb with dose) pays off in the scarring chapter

scenes.narration: If you have been told you have a fatty liver and you are wondering whether tirzepatide helps:

visual.stock_query: calm woman reading lab letter kitchen

scenes.retention_device: Searched question repeated word for word, in 'you' terms, at t=0

scenes.narration: in one randomized Phase Two trial in adults with MASH and moderate or advanced liver scarring, more people on tirzepatide than on placebo had their MASH resolve, without their scarring getting worse, on a liver biopsy after fifty-two weeks.
scenes.on_screen_text: More MASH resolved, scarring not worse

visual.stock_query: hopeful doctor showing chart to woman

scenes.narration: It is not an approved use, so it is one to talk through with your doctor.
Here are the numbers. MASH resolved in ten percent of people on placebo, versus forty-four, fifty-six and sixty-two percent on the lowest, middle and highest tirzepatide doses tested.

visual.stat_label: MASH resolved, no fibrosis worsening: placebo vs tirzepatide, 52 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff: the headline number at about 21–30 s

scenes.narration: That is encouraging. But it is one mid-stage trial, and there is more to understand before it means anything for you.
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore turn into the deeper story

scenes.narration: Next: what MASH actually is, why the liver stores fat at all, and what an MRI study found in type two diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Promise of what the viewer will get

scenes.narration: And one result in this trial did not climb with the dose the way you might expect.

visual.stock_query: curious woman raising eyebrow at graph

scenes.retention_device: Open loop (pays off in 'The scarring surprise')

scenes.narration: First, the words on that report.
Imagine Dana, forty-eight, who has type two diabetes. A routine scan comes back with a phrase she did not expect: fatty liver.
If that phrase made you feel judged or worried, you are not alone. And the biology behind it is more than a willpower story.
Liver societies renamed the condition. What was called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease became MASLD: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
The name says what it is: extra fat in the liver, plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, such as a larger waist, high blood sugar or high blood pressure.

items: e.g. waist, blood sugar, blood pressure

scenes.narration: MASH is the more active form. On a biopsy, the fat comes with signs of liver cell injury and inflammation, and that activity can drive scarring over time.
How common is fatty liver? A large review put its global prevalence at about thirty-two percent, under its older name. That is roughly one adult in three.

visual.stat_label: Estimated global adult prevalence, fatty liver (older name)

scenes.narration: Doctors grade the scarring, called fibrosis, from stage zero, meaning none, up to stage four, which is cirrhosis. The tirzepatide biopsy trial enrolled stages two and three.
Why does that scale matter? In a long-term study of six hundred nineteen people with fatty liver disease, fibrosis stage, and no other biopsy feature, was linked with long-term outcomes.

visual.stat_label: People followed: fibrosis stage linked to outcomes

scenes.narration: Hold on to that. Scarring is where this story takes its most surprising turn.
So how does fat end up in the liver in the first place?
Not only from your plate. In one small study of nine people with fatty liver, researchers tagged fat with non-radioactive tracers, like dropping a different dye into three streams.

visual.stock_query: three colored streams into cartoon house

scenes.retention_device: Micro-story about a clever study design

scenes.narration: About fifty-nine percent of the stored liver fat came from fatty acids already circulating in the blood, released from fat stores.

visual.stat_label: Stored liver fat from blood fatty acids
visual.stock_query: blue stream flowing into storage room

scenes.narration: About a quarter was made fresh inside the liver, from carbohydrates. And only about fifteen percent came straight from dietary fat.

visual.stat_label: Made in liver · from dietary fat
visual.stock_query: tiny factory making boxes inside room

scenes.narration: Here is where insulin resistance comes in. When the body responds poorly to insulin, fat tissue releases more fatty acids into the blood, and high insulin levels push the liver to make more fat of its own.
scenes.retention_device: The why, explained like a friend

scenes.narration: Think of the liver as a storage room with deliveries arriving through two doors, while the trucks heading out cannot keep up.
That is why fatty liver is strongly linked with excess weight around the middle and with type two diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Ties biology to the viewer's situation

scenes.narration: So what do liver guidelines recommend first?
Lifestyle changes: an eating pattern that supports weight loss, regular physical activity, and an honest conversation about alcohol.
In that guidance, weight loss is central, and greater weight loss is linked with greater improvement in the liver.

visual.stock_query: rising bar chart with smiling liver icon

scenes.narration: To be clear, these habits are recommended for fatty liver in general. They are not proven as add-ons to tirzepatide for the liver.

visual.myth: These habits are proven add-ons to tirzepatide for the liver
visual.fact: Recommended for fatty liver in general; not tested with tirzepatide

scenes.narration: Back to Dana. Her obvious question: does a medicine that lowers blood sugar and weight also change what is happening in her liver?
Two trials looked at that in very different ways. One used a scanner. The other looked at liver tissue under a microscope.

visual.stock_query: MRI scanner and microscope side by side

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: new open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: First, the scanner.

In adults with type two diabetes on metformin, with or without an SGLT-two inhibitor, the two higher tirzepatide doses tested, pooled, lowered liver fat content on MRI by eight point zero nine percentage points over fifty-two weeks.

visual.stat_label: Liver fat on MRI, pooled tirzepatide, 52 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Result and population in one sentence

scenes.narration: On insulin degludec, the comparison treatment, liver fat content fell by three point three eight percentage points.

visual.stat_label: Liver fat on MRI, insulin degludec, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: Those are percentage points, because MRI reports liver fat as a share of the liver. Both arms lost liver fat, and the tirzepatide arms lost more.

visual.stock_query: two bars shrinking side by side

scenes.narration: This was a substudy of the SURPASS-three trial, and it was open-label, so people knew which treatment they were on.
Here is the limit. An MRI measures fat. It cannot show whether MASH resolved, or whether scarring changed.

visual.myth: Less liver fat on MRI means MASH resolved
visual.fact: MRI measures fat, not MASH or scarring

scenes.retention_device: But-turn that sets up the next chapter

scenes.narration: For that, you need a tiny sample of liver under a microscope. Which brings us to the biopsy trial.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: cliffhanger into the main trial

scenes.narration: Next, the trial behind the headline.

In SYNERGY-NASH, among one hundred ninety adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage two or three scarring, MASH resolved without worsening of scarring in ten percent on placebo after fifty-two weeks.

visual.stat_label: Placebo: MASH resolved, no fibrosis worsening, 52 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Result and population in one sentence

scenes.narration: On tirzepatide, it was forty-four, fifty-six and sixty-two percent, on the lowest, middle and highest doses tested.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the headline number in detail

scenes.narration: This result did climb with the dose. It was a Phase Two, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: a mid-sized, dose-finding step that usually comes before larger Phase Three trials.
scenes.retention_device: Sets contrast for the open loop

scenes.narration: So what does resolved mean? It means the follow-up biopsy no longer met the criteria for MASH: no ballooned, injured liver cells, and little or no inflammation, and scarring had not got worse.

visual.myth: MASH resolved = liver is back to normal
visual.fact: Biopsy no longer met MASH criteria; scarring not worse

scenes.narration: Think of a building inspection. Several features are scored together, and the liver has to pass the whole checklist, not just one line.
In plain terms: about one in ten passed on placebo, versus roughly four to six in ten on tirzepatide.

visual.stat_label: MASH resolved, no fibrosis worsening: placebo vs tirzepatide, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: On tolerability, the most common adverse events on tirzepatide were gastrointestinal, and most were mild or moderate in severity.
But resolving MASH was only the main goal. The result I promised you at the start is about scarring.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: callback to the open loop

scenes.narration: Here is that result.
As a secondary outcome, the trial measured scarring improving by at least one stage without MASH getting worse.
On placebo, thirty percent improved. On tirzepatide, it was fifty-five, fifty-one and fifty-one percent, from the lowest dose tested to the highest.

visual.stat_label: Fibrosis improved ≥1 stage: placebo vs tirzepatide

scenes.narration: Notice the pattern. The three doses landed close together, with the lowest dose slightly highest. Unlike the MASH result, this one did not climb with dose.

visual.stock_query: woman pointing at flat line surprised

scenes.narration: Why? This trial cannot say. Fifty-two weeks is a short window, and a Phase Two secondary outcome is a signal to test, not a final answer.
Notice the placebo number too. Thirty percent improved without the drug, a reminder that biopsy readings can vary and placebo groups can improve too.

visual.stock_query: placebo pill bottle with question mark

scenes.retention_device: But here's where it gets interesting

scenes.narration: Still, remember that long-term study: fibrosis stage was the biopsy feature linked with outcomes. So this is the signal worth watching in larger, longer trials.
And one trial cannot tell us how much of the effect came from weight loss itself, and how much from anything else.

visual.stock_query: two puzzle pieces not yet joined

scenes.narration: So if the evidence is promising, why is fatty liver not an approved use for tirzepatide? It comes down to the label.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: question bridging to the next chapter

scenes.narration: Here is what the labels actually list.
Section one of the Mounjaro label lists two uses. First: alongside diet and exercise, to improve blood sugar control in adults and children ten years and older with type two diabetes.

Second: to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, meaning cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke, in adults with type two diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
scenes.on_screen_text: Mounjaro use 2: heart events, high-risk type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: Section one of the Zepbound label lists two uses, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

visual.stock_query: woman reading label at kitchen counter

scenes.narration: To reduce excess body weight and keep it off long term, in adults with obesity, or with overweight and at least one weight-related condition. And to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

items: Weight: adults with obesity, or overweight + weight-related condition
Moderate to severe sleep apnea, adults with obesity

scenes.narration: Fatty liver, MASLD and MASH are not on either list.

visual.myth: Tirzepatide is approved for fatty liver
visual.fact: Not in Mounjaro or Zepbound Section 1

scenes.narration: For context, FDA has approved semaglutide, sold as Wegovy, under accelerated approval, for adults with noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
So for tirzepatide, the liver is still a research question, and a fair one to raise with your doctor.
If you take tirzepatide for an approved use, two safety points from the Medication Guide matter.

Stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area, your abdomen, that will not go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your abdomen to your back.

items: Severe stomach-area pain that won't go away
Stop using it; call your provider right away

scenes.narration: Your risk of low blood sugar may be higher if you use it with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and low blood sugar has also been reported in people without type two diabetes.
scenes.on_screen_text: Low blood sugar: may be higher

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't stop or change on your own

scenes.narration: And the hopeful part: there is a lot you and your doctor can do while the research catches up.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter ends on hope, not a warning

scenes.narration: Here is the whole picture.
On biopsy, in one Phase Two trial, MASH resolved without scarring getting worse in roughly one in ten people on placebo, versus four to six in ten on tirzepatide.

visual.stat_label: MASH resolved, no fibrosis worsening: placebo vs tirzepatide, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: On MRI, in type two diabetes, liver fat fell more on tirzepatide than on insulin degludec. And as a secondary outcome, scarring improved more often than on placebo, with no clear dose pattern.

items: MRI: liver fat fell more than on degludec
Scarring: better than placebo, no dose pattern

scenes.narration: If that phrase on your report made you feel blamed, remember the biology: fat reaches the liver from several directions, and insulin resistance is a big part of why.
If you are referred to a liver specialist, a hepatologist, three questions are worth asking.

items: How will we track my liver?
visual.stock_query: woman holding question list at clinic

scenes.narration: One: what stage is my scarring, and how was it measured?
Two: how will we track my liver over time?
Three: which treatments fit my stage and my other conditions?
Back to Dana. She does not leave with a promise. She leaves knowing her stage, how it will be tracked, and what to ask next.
Fatty liver is not an approved use for tirzepatide. It is a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe, so it passes. I found no fact errors and no safety problems. There are 5 minor wording and sourcing fixes below.

What I checked:
- **SYNERGY-NASH (S1, NEJM 2024):** 190 adults with F2–F3 fibrosis. MASH resolved without fibrosis worsening in 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% on tirzepatide. Fibrosis improved by at least 1 stage in 30% on placebo vs 55%, 51% and 51%. Matches the script.
- **SURPASS-3 MRI (S2):** liver fat fell −8.09 points on pooled tirzepatide vs −3.38 on degludec. Matches.
- **Other studies:** Riazi prevalence of 32.4% (S4), Angulo's 619 patients with fibrosis as the only histologic feature linked to outcomes (S5), and Donnelly's 9 patients split 59.0% / 26.1% / 14.9% (S6). All match.
- **Mounjaro label (S9, revised 8/2026):** Section 1 lists glycemic control in adults and children 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, plus the MACE indication. Matches s57–s58.
- **Zepbound label (S11, revised 8/2026):** Section 1 lists weight reduction and moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Section 5.7 reports low blood sugar in adults without type 2 diabetes. Matches s60 and s66.
- **Approval status:** tirzepatide is still not approved for MASH, so the "not an approved use" line is correct.

Framing is right throughout: the scope stays at one Phase 2 trial, fibrosis is called a secondary outcome, MRI is described as measuring fat only, and the lifestyle advice is labelled as not tested with tirzepatide. The safety lines follow the Medication Guide, and "that emergency sign" is correctly singular.

**Not confirmed:** both PDF sources (S10 Mounjaro Medication Guide, S12 Wegovy label) loaded, but I couldn't read the text inside them. I didn't confirm S10's exact wording, and S12 has no revised date yet. Both are listed in the issues.

**Verified sources list:** it holds the 10 sources I confirmed directly. S10 and S12 are left off because I couldn't read their text.

issues.claim: "If you've been told…" / "It isn't an approved use, so it's one to talk through…" / "There's a video I'd watch next…"
issues.problem: House rule: no contractions in narration except in the fixed safety lines.
issues.fix: s1: "If you have been told you have a fatty liver and you are wondering whether tirzepatide helps:" s3: "It is not an approved use, so it is one to talk through with your doctor." s80: "There is a video I would watch next, linked in the description."

issues.claim: "placebo groups in liver trials often improve too"
issues.problem: This is a general claim about liver trials, but its only source is the single trial S1. S1 shows the 30% placebo figure; it does not support "often".
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "Notice the placebo number too. Thirty percent improved without the drug, a reminder that biopsy readings can vary and placebo groups can improve too."

issues.claim: "The lowest dose had the highest number."
issues.problem: The gaps are small (55% vs 51% vs 51%) and the trial didn't compare the doses with each other. A viewer could read this as "the lower dose works better".
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "Notice the pattern. The three doses landed close together, with the lowest dose slightly highest. Unlike the MASH result, this one did not climb with dose."

issues.claim: Wegovy Prescribing Information, Section 1: MASH indication (2025)
issues.problem: No revised date is given, which breaks the sourcing rule. The PDF loaded, but I couldn't read its text to check the date.
issues.fix: Look up the live revised date on the Wegovy PI or DailyMed. Then change the title to: "Wegovy (semaglutide) injection Prescribing Information, Section 1 (Indications and Usage): MASH indication, revised [live date]".

issues.claim: Mounjaro Medication Guide wording for pancreatitis and low blood sugar, revised 8/2026
issues.problem: The PDF URL works, but I couldn't read its text. So I didn't confirm the 8/2026 date or the exact sentences used in s65 and s66. The wording matches the standard Mounjaro Medication Guide.
issues.fix: Before publishing, open the PDF and check two things. First, the revised date matches 8/2026. thumbnail.reasoning:
All three are legible at phone size with short, non-overlapping text and a single focal point, and none of them give away the answer (none state whether tirzepatide helps fatty liver or is approved for it), so no hard caps apply for "gives the answer."

#0 ("LIVER FAT?"): Clean and legible, but the mascot's expression (closed eyes, soft smile) reads as calm/content rather than worried, which undercuts the tension the question "LIVER FAT?" is trying to create for someone newly worried about a diagnosis. It's a mild mismatch, not a full smile-on-bad-news contradiction, but it blunts the emotional pull. Curiosity gap is decent but generic phrasing is less scroll-stopping than a concrete number.

#1 ("10% VS 62%"): Strongest curiosity gap — a specific, surprising number pairing forces a "62% of what?" reaction, which is exactly the kind of pattern-interrupt that beats a generic question in a crowded health feed. "PHASE 2 TRIAL" and "ON A LIVER BIOPSY?" correctly scope the claim without revealing the result, so it stays honest to the content (SYNERGY-NASH) while promising a payoff. Clipboard + arrow is a clear single focal point, text is large and uncluttered at phone size.

#2 ("APPROVED FOR LIVER?"): Good expectation-violation hook and the worried box-face emotion matches the tension of the question well. Legible and clean. Slightly less concrete/numeric than #1, so marginally lower curiosity pull, but a strong alternative.

Given legibility ties (all ~9) and no disqualifying issues, #1 wins on CTR because concrete, surprising numbers typically outperform open-ended questions for click-through, while staying fully honest to the SYNERGY-NASH data the video will unpack.

But the thumbnail "MASH RESOLVED 10%-62%" puts placebo (10%) and the top tirzepatide dose (62%) into one range, which misstates the drug's result. That's misleading for a use that isn't approved, and nobody has fixed it.
